newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian protesters march on, Socialists squirm.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian protesters march on, Socialists squirm.

text.p: Bulgaria's opposition parties planned more mass protests on Saturday to pile pressure on the divided and dispirited ruling Socialists to quit and hold elections.
Students and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) will stage three marches and a mass rally in central Sofia to keep up their anti-government protests for a 27th day.
The opposition, saying the country is sinking into economic chaos, is trying to force the discredited Socialists to call a general election nearly two years ahead of schedule.

The students, who have kept their demonstrations lively with colourful street theatre, have taken to dancing through Sofia's central streets, blocking key intersections for 30 minutes and then moving on.

Some 1,000 UDF supporters blockaded the main southern road and rail links to Greece for a fourth day on Saturday. The UDF said on Saturday it would reinforce the blockades and offered people free rides to them from Sofia.
About 100 local riot police stood nearby while tyres burned in the middle of the highway south of Sofia. Pop music blared and protesters were in a festive mood despite the cold.
President Petar Stoyanov met central bank governor Lyubomir Filipov on Saturday to discuss a letter from International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Michel Camdessus.

Camdessus said the IMF was ready to help Bulgaria through its economic crisis as soon as a valid government was in place. He urged Stoyanov to impress on all political parties the high social cost of delay.
The IMF has been holding up a $115 million standby credit, saying urgent reforms must be carried out -- notably closing loss-making state firms and rapid privatisation.
The Socialists, formerly the communists, are struggling to form a new government to deal with the economic collapse -- with inflation estimated at 50 percent a month and rising.
They will hold a special meeting of Socialist parliamentary deputies, coalition partners and the Supreme Council of the Socialist Party on Sunday to chart their next move.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, who received a mandate to form a government, has until Tuesday to choose his cabinet and face a vote of confidence in the 240-seat parliament.
But in view of the widespread popular opposition, he has appeared half-hearted in his efforts and has offered several times to stand aside, or even to return the mandate.
He told Reuters in an interview on Friday he was willing to accept a coalition cabinet formed under the aegis of Stoyanov.
"I don't mind if it is formed under the leadership of the president," he said. "I am ready to return my mandate if such a government is formed."

But he then postponed a scheduled meeting with Stoyanov, apparently under pressure from hardliners in his party. He said later he had to give Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov time for more talks with other political parties.

The Socialists, elected for a four-year term in 1994, have overseen a caretaker cabinet since December when Zhan Videnov resigned as prime minister. His resignation followed a crushing defeat for the Socialists in November's presidential election.
The Socialists have an absolute majority in parliament but it is clear that they have little popular support to carry out vital economic reform.
Thousands of demonstrators marched through central Sofia for a 26th day on Friday, blowing whistles, chanting "victory" and delighting in mocking the beleaguered Socialists.
Pop singers belted out tunes while thousands of protesters rocked in front of Alexander Nevski cathedral. Black-robed Orthodox priests clapped to the music on the front steps.
Students, teachers, nurses, miners, transport and oil refinery workers staged stoppages or colourful protests during the day. Miners appeared wearing helmets with lights switched on in central Sofia.
